programs.name: Assisted Living Facility Financing
programs.description: Licensed residential care facilities providing personal care services, medication management, and daily living assistance to seniors who cannot live independently but do not require skilled nursing care. The largest segment of the seniors housing market by deal volume. Lenders underwrite operator credit, state licensing risk, occupancy ramp, and staffing cost structures.
typical_stack: HUD 232/223(f) permanent loan for stabilized facilities with 90 percent or better occupancy
Permanent loan: life insurance company or CMBS for institutional-quality stabilized facilities
Bridge: specialty seniors housing debt fund or regional bank for lease-up and value-add
Construction loan: HUD 232 new construction or specialty seniors housing bank

key_features.tenant_profile: Seniors requiring assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs), private pay and limited Medicaid mix
key_features.typical_lease_term: Month-to-month residency agreements with strong retention for residents who can afford quality care
key_features.building_specs: Residential-style construction, 40 to 150 units typical, common dining, activity spaces, secured memory care wings
key_features.most_competitive_lender: HUD 232 for stabilized fully licensed facilities, life companies for institutional operators in primary markets
key_features.ltv_ranges: 80 to 85 percent HUD, 65 to 70 percent life co, 70 to 75 percent CMBS, 75 to 80 percent bridge
key_features.rate_environment_2026: HUD 232 fixed 40-year at 5.5 to 6.5 percent all-in, life co 175 to 250 over 10-year, bridge SOFR plus 350 to 550

seo.meta_template: Assisted living facility financing in {city}. HUD 232, life company, CMBS, and bridge lenders for licensed assisted living acquisitions, construction, and refinance.

programs.name: Memory Care Facility Financing
programs.description: Specialized secured residential care facilities serving seniors with Alzheimer's disease, dementia, and related cognitive impairments. Highest-acuity seniors housing segment outside skilled nursing. Higher staffing ratios, secured perimeters, and purpose-built layouts command premium rates and attract lenders who understand operator quality and state licensure. Demand is structural given aging demographics.
typical_stack: Bridge: specialty seniors housing debt fund for acquisition and lease-up of stand-alone memory care
HUD 232/223(f) for stabilized memory care with strong operator history
Permanent loan: life company or CMBS for institutional operators in primary markets
Construction: specialty seniors housing bank or HUD 232 new construction for purpose-built facilities

key_features.tenant_profile: Residents with Alzheimer's, dementia, and other cognitive conditions requiring 24-hour supervised care
key_features.building_specs: Fully secured perimeter, wayfinding design, sensory spaces, secured courtyard, 40 to 80 units typical, clustered unit neighborhoods
key_features.staffing_cost_weight: Staffing is 55 to 70 percent of operating expenses, making operator quality the dominant underwriting variable
key_features.most_competitive_lender: Specialty seniors housing debt funds for lease-up, HUD 232 for stabilized with licensed operator
key_features.ltv_ranges: 70 to 80 percent HUD 232 on stabilized, 60 to 70 percent life co, 75 to 85 percent bridge with recourse
key_features.rate_environment_2026: Bridge SOFR plus 400 to 600 reflecting operator risk premium, permanent HUD or life co 175 to 275 over for stabilized

seo.meta_template: Memory care facility financing in {city}. Specialty seniors housing lenders, HUD 232, and bridge capital for Alzheimer's and dementia care acquisitions and development.

programs.name: Independent Living Community Financing
programs.description: Age-restricted communities (55+ or 62+) providing lifestyle amenities, social programming, and optional dining for active seniors who do not require personal care services. The most real-estate-like seniors housing segment. Underwriting resembles multifamily more than healthcare, and lenders underwrite location, amenity quality, competitive positioning, and management quality rather than healthcare acuity.
typical_stack: Permanent loan: Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac for qualifying 55-plus communities meeting agency criteria
Life insurance company for institutional-quality stabilized campuses
CMBS for stabilized assets in primary and secondary markets
Bridge: debt fund or regional bank for value-add repositioning and lease-up
Construction loan: national bank or regional bank for ground-up development

key_features.tenant_profile: Active seniors aged 55 to 75, typically homeowners transitioning to maintenance-free lifestyle living
key_features.typical_lease_term: Annual leases with strong 80 to 90 percent renewal rates among established communities
key_features.building_specs: Apartment-style or cottage configurations, resort-style amenities, clubhouse, fitness, pools, dining optional
key_features.most_competitive_lender: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac for qualifying 55-plus with proper income and age restrictions
key_features.ltv_ranges: 65 to 75 percent agency, 60 to 70 percent life co, 70 to 75 percent CMBS, up to 80 percent bridge
key_features.rate_environment_2026: Agency IL 175 to 225 over 10-year, life co 150 to 200 over 10-year for Class A stabilized

seo.meta_template: Independent living community financing in {city}. Agency, life company, CMBS, and construction lenders for 55-plus and active senior communities.

cities.name: Los Angeles
cities.market_notes: Los Angeles is one of the nation's top seniors housing markets, driven by a large and affluent aging population, high median household wealth, and strong private-pay demand in the West Side, San Fernando Valley, and Conejo Valley. Land and construction costs are among the highest in the country, making new supply constrained and underwriting premiums on existing stabilized assets sustainable.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies actively compete for Class A stabilized assisted living and independent living in primary LA submarkets. HUD 232 is the preferred long-term takeout for stabilized assisted living and memory care with strong operators. Specialty seniors housing debt funds and some regional banks provide bridge financing for lease-up and value-add. CMBS is active for mid-market stabilized assets in the $10M to $40M range.
cities.submarkets: West LA and Bel Air, Calabasas and Agoura Hills, Pasadena and San Marino, Torrance and Redondo Beach, Sherman Oaks and Encino, Santa Clarita

cities.name: Phoenix
cities.market_notes: Phoenix is one of the largest and fastest-growing seniors housing markets in the country, fueled by Arizona's status as a retirement destination for Midwestern and Californian seniors seeking warm climate, lower cost of living, and resort-style amenities. Scottsdale, Paradise Valley, and East Valley have among the highest concentrations of Class A independent living and assisted living in the Sun Belt.
cities.active_lender_commentary: HUD 232 is heavily used in Phoenix for stabilized assisted living and memory care with qualified operators. Life companies compete for Class A facilities in Scottsdale and the East Valley. CMBS is active across the metro for mid-market stabilized assets. Specialty seniors housing debt funds provide bridge on lease-up communities throughout the Valley. Regional Arizona banks active on construction for regional operators.
cities.submarkets: Scottsdale and Paradise Valley, Chandler and Gilbert, Peoria and Sun City, Mesa and Tempe, North Phoenix and Anthem, Surprise and Sun City West

cities.name: Dallas
cities.market_notes: DFW is a top-five seniors housing market nationally with strong private-pay demand across Plano, Colleyville, Southlake, and Frisco. Texas has no income tax, a favorable regulatory environment for seniors housing operators, and strong household formation and in-migration that drives long-term demand for age-restricted communities. Memory care is an active sub-segment tied to the suburban growth of North Dallas.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies and CMBS conduits are the primary permanent lenders for stabilized Dallas seniors housing. HUD 232 actively used by operators seeking long-term fixed-rate debt. Regional Texas banks and national bank construction desks active for ground-up development in North Dallas growth corridors. Specialty seniors housing debt funds provide bridge for lease-up communities in suburban submarkets.
cities.submarkets: Plano and Frisco, Southlake and Colleyville, Allen and McKinney, Far North Dallas and Carrollton, Flower Mound and Lewisville, Fort Worth and Keller

cities.name: Tampa
cities.market_notes: Tampa and the broader Tampa Bay area are core Florida seniors housing markets, supported by strong retiree in-migration, Florida's tax-friendly environment, and the area's appeal to active Baby Boomers. Pinellas County (St. Petersburg and Clearwater) has among the highest senior population concentrations in Florida, making independent living and assisted living demand structurally strong across the market.
cities.active_lender_commentary: HUD 232 is widely used across the Tampa Bay market for stabilized assisted living and memory care facilities. Life companies and CMBS compete for Class A independent living and assisted living in Hillsborough and Pinellas. Florida-focused regional banks active on construction and acquisitions. Specialty seniors housing debt funds provide bridge financing for lease-up and value-add throughout the metro.
cities.submarkets: Carrollwood and Northdale, Westchase and Town 'n' Country, New Tampa and Wesley Chapel, St. Petersburg and Pinellas Park, Clearwater and Dunedin, Brandon and Riverview

cities.name: Miami
cities.market_notes: Miami has a uniquely affluent and international aging population that drives premium private-pay demand for high-end seniors housing. Coral Gables, Pinecrest, and Aventura have concentrations of Class A independent living and assisted living serving Latin American and domestic retirees. Memory care demand is strong given the demographics of South Florida's older Cuban, Venezuelan, and domestic retiree communities.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies compete for Class A stabilized seniors housing in Coral Gables and Aventura. HUD 232 used for qualifying licensed assisted living and memory care facilities. CMBS active for mid-market stabilized assets across Miami-Dade and Broward. Florida-based regional banks provide construction financing. Specialty seniors housing debt funds active for lease-up and repositioning.
cities.submarkets: Coral Gables and South Miami, Pinecrest and Palmetto Bay, Aventura and Hallandale Beach, Boca Raton and Delray Beach, Doral and West Miami, Fort Lauderdale and Pompano Beach

cities.name: Denver
cities.market_notes: Denver's outdoor-lifestyle appeal and quality of life attract early retirees seeking active seniors communities, making it one of the stronger Mountain West seniors housing markets. The aging population in Jefferson County, Douglas County, and the northern I-25 corridor drives demand for assisted living and memory care. Colorado's regulatory environment for seniors housing is manageable compared to California, making development viable.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life companies and CMBS compete for stabilized Class A seniors housing in Douglas County, south Denver, and the northern suburbs. HUD 232 is used selectively for qualifying assisted living with strong operators. Colorado-based regional banks active on construction and bridge financing. Specialty seniors housing debt funds provide lease-up bridge across the metro.
cities.submarkets: Greenwood Village and Centennial, Parker and Castle Rock, Highlands Ranch and Lone Tree, Lakewood and Golden, Westminster and Broomfield, Fort Collins adjacent

cities.name: New York
cities.market_notes: New York City and its surrounding metro area represent one of the most complex senior living financing markets in the country, driven by an aging baby boomer population of over 1.4 million residents aged 65 and older across the five boroughs and suburban counties. Occupancy rates for stabilized assisted living and memory care facilities in the metro have recovered strongly post-pandemic, with many properties in Westchester, Long Island, and outer boroughs running above 90% occupancy due to severely constrained supply driven by high land costs and restrictive zoning. Lenders remain cautious about new construction in core Manhattan due to extraordinary development costs and thin margins, but are selectively active on acquisitions and refinances of stabilized facilities in high-barrier suburban submarkets where demographics and household wealth support strong private-pay revenue.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Debt funds and regional banks including New York Community Bank affiliates and institutions like Valley National and Investors Bank are among the most active capital sources for stabilized senior living acquisitions and bridge financing in the New York metro, attracted by the strong private-pay demographics in suburban submarkets. HUD 232 agency financing remains highly sought after for permanent debt on qualifying facilities given the long-term fixed rates and non-recourse structure, particularly in Long Island and Westchester where project economics support the underwriting thresholds.
cities.submarkets: Westchester County, Long Island, Brooklyn, Queens, The Bronx, Staten Island, Northern New Jersey, Fairfield County CT

cities.name: Houston
cities.market_notes: Houston's senior living market benefits from one of the fastest-growing 65-plus populations in the nation, driven by sustained in-migration, a large medical infrastructure anchored by the Texas Medical Center, and a relatively affordable cost of living that supports private-pay assisted living demand. Occupancy rates across the metro have been recovering steadily post-pandemic, with stabilized Class A communities in affluent suburban corridors reporting occupancy in the low-to-mid 90s, while newer lease-up properties in overbuilt pockets face more pressure. The development pipeline remains active in high-growth suburban nodes like The Woodlands and Sugar Land, which keeps lenders selective about sponsorship quality and pre-leasing velocity before committing to construction financing.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional and community banks headquartered in Texas, including institutions with strong Houston footprints, are the most consistent construction and bridge lenders for assisted living and memory care projects given their familiarity with local operators and the state's regulatory environment. HUD and agency lenders remain highly competitive for stabilized, cash-flowing facilities seeking long-term permanent financing, particularly for larger independent living and assisted living communities that meet occupancy thresholds.
cities.submarkets: The Woodlands, Sugar Land, Katy, Galleria/Uptown, Medical Center/NRG Area, Pearland, Cypress, Clear Lake

cities.name: Atlanta
cities.market_notes: Atlanta's senior living financing market benefits from one of the fastest-growing 75-plus populations in the Southeast, fueled by net in-migration from higher-cost metros and the region's relatively affordable cost of living. Occupancy across stabilized assisted living and memory care assets in the metro has rebounded to the low-to-mid 80s percentage range post-pandemic, with purpose-built memory care facilities in affluent northern suburbs showing occupancy above 90 percent. The development pipeline remains active in the Alpharetta and Sandy Springs corridors, which draws lender scrutiny around lease-up risk, though stabilized assets with strong operator track records continue to attract competitive financing terms.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Regions Bank and Truist are among the most active construction and bridge lenders for Atlanta senior living projects, leveraging their deep Southeast relationships and familiarity with local operators. Debt funds such as Benefit Street Partners and Cerberus are stepping in for value-add and lease-up bridge scenarios where traditional balance sheet lenders require higher stabilization thresholds, while HUD 232 agency financing remains the go-to execution for stabilized assets seeking long-term fixed-rate debt.
cities.submarkets: Sandy Springs, Alpharetta, Buckhead, Marietta, Decatur, Peachtree City, Dunwoody, Johns Creek

cities.name: Chicago
cities.market_notes: Chicago's senior living and assisted living market benefits from one of the largest 75-plus population bases in the Midwest, with Cook, DuPage, and Lake counties driving consistent absorption across assisted living and memory care product types. Occupancy across stabilized facilities in the metro has recovered into the low-to-mid 80s percent range, with newer purpose-built communities in affluent suburban corridors outperforming older urban stock. Development activity remains measured due to construction cost pressures and zoning complexity in the city proper, which is keeping lenders cautiously optimistic about well-located, operationally proven assets while remaining selective on ground-up projects.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Wintrust, Byline Bank, and Heartland Bank are among the most active financing sources for stabilized assisted living and memory care facilities in the Chicago metro, favoring experienced operators with clean survey histories and strong occupancy trends. HUD 232 agency financing remains highly competitive for refinancing stabilized properties, while debt funds are stepping in to fill bridge lending gaps for value-add acquisitions and lease-up deals where conventional lenders require seasoned cash flow.
cities.submarkets: Naperville, Schaumburg, Oak Brook, Evanston, Arlington Heights, Lincoln Park, Orland Park, Lake Forest

cities.name: Seattle
cities.market_notes: Seattle's rapidly aging population, driven by retiring tech sector workers and long-term residents in one of the nation's most expensive metros, is creating strong sustained demand for senior living and assisted living facilities across the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue MSA. Occupancy rates in stabilized assisted living and memory care properties have been trending upward, recovering well past post-pandemic lows, with Class A facilities in affluent eastside suburbs like Bellevue and Redmond reporting occupancies above 90%. The development pipeline remains constrained by Seattle's high construction costs, zoning complexity, and labor market pressures, which limits new supply and supports rent growth but also gives lenders pause on ground-up construction financing.
cities.active_lender_commentary: HUD and FHA lenders remain the most active financing source for stabilized senior living and assisted living facilities in Seattle due to the strong operational fundamentals and agency-backed rate advantages, while regional banks such as Banner Bank and HomeStreet Bank remain competitive for bridge and value-add deals where borrowers need execution speed and relationship-driven underwriting. Debt funds have stepped in to fill construction and transitional financing gaps as traditional banks have pulled back on new development amid elevated construction cost risk.
cities.submarkets: Bellevue, Redmond, Shoreline, Tacoma, Kirkland, Renton, Bothell, Federal Way

cities.name: San Diego
cities.market_notes: San Diego's senior living and assisted living financing market benefits from one of the strongest demographic tailwinds in California, with the 75-plus population growing rapidly across the metro's affluent coastal and inland communities. Occupancy rates at stabilized facilities have largely recovered to pre-pandemic levels, frequently exceeding 88 to 92 percent in premium submarkets like La Jolla and Rancho Bernardo, driven by high household wealth, a desirable retirement climate, and limited new supply constrained by zoning restrictions and elevated land costs. The development pipeline remains thin relative to demand, making existing licensed facilities highly attractive acquisition targets and encouraging lenders to underwrite stabilized deals with confidence, though construction financing remains selective given rising construction costs and entitlement complexity.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks with California presence, including institutions like Western Alliance and Pacific Premier, are among the most active lenders for stabilized assisted living and memory care acquisitions in San Diego, attracted by strong operator performance and high barriers to new supply. Debt funds are stepping in aggressively for bridge-to-agency executions on value-add and lease-up assets, while HUD and Fannie Mae programs remain the go-to permanent financing options for qualified operators seeking long-term fixed-rate debt on larger facilities.
cities.submarkets: La Jolla, Rancho Bernardo, Carlsbad, Chula Vista, Vista, Escondido, Encinitas, El Cajon

cities.name: San Francisco
cities.market_notes: San Francisco's senior living and assisted living market benefits from one of the highest concentrations of high-net-worth seniors in the nation, driven by decades of tech and finance wealth accumulation, creating strong demand for premium memory care and assisted living product. Occupancy rates across the metro have rebounded solidly post-pandemic, hovering in the low-to-mid 80s percent range for stabilized assets, with luxury and continuing care retirement communities performing above market averages given the affluent local demographic. Development remains constrained by San Francisco's notoriously restrictive entitlement process, high construction costs, and limited available land, which limits new supply and supports valuations for existing well-located facilities across the broader Bay Area metro.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Debt funds and regional banks such as Western Alliance and Pacific Premier Bank are among the most active capital sources for senior living and assisted living facilities in the San Francisco metro, attracted by the strong income demographics and supply-constrained environment, while agency lenders including HUD and Fannie Mae remain competitive for stabilized, cash-flowing assisted living and memory care assets meeting occupancy thresholds. Life companies are selectively engaged on higher-quality, well-stabilized facilities in established submarkets like San Mateo and Palo Alto where long-term income stability aligns with their underwriting preferences.
cities.submarkets: Oakland, San Mateo, Palo Alto, Mission Bay, Marin County, Walnut Creek, Fremont, Concord

cities.name: Austin
cities.market_notes: Austin's rapid population growth, fueled by technology sector relocations and an influx of younger professionals aging into the senior cohort over the coming decade, is creating strong long-term demand fundamentals for senior living and assisted living facilities across the metro. Occupancy rates at stabilized Austin-area facilities have trended upward toward the low-to-mid 80s percent range as pandemic-era disruptions fade, though a notable pipeline of new memory care and assisted living projects in suburban corridors like Cedar Park and Georgetown is adding supply that lenders are monitoring carefully. Lenders remain generally constructive on Austin senior living given demographic tailwinds and income growth, but are underwriting new construction more conservatively due to elevated construction costs, extended lease-up timelines, and competition from recently delivered projects.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Debt funds and regional banks are the most active capital sources for Austin senior living and assisted living financing right now, with debt funds stepping in aggressively on bridge-to-stabilization loans for value-add acquisitions and lease-up assets where agency execution is not yet available, while regional banks like Frost Bank and Texas Capital are providing construction and mini-perm financing to experienced regional operators with proven track records. HUD 232 and Fannie Mae remain the preferred long-term execution for stabilized facilities, though borrowers should anticipate longer processing timelines given current agency volume.
cities.submarkets: Cedar Park, Round Rock, Georgetown, The Domain, Pflugerville, Leander, South Austin, Bee Cave

cities.name: Nashville
cities.market_notes: Nashville's senior living and assisted living facility financing market benefits from a powerful combination of rapid population growth, a dominant healthcare industry anchored by HCA Healthcare and Vanderbilt Health, and strong in-migration of retirees drawn by Tennessee's no state income tax and high quality of life. Occupancy rates across the metro have rebounded solidly post-pandemic, with stabilized assets in affluent submarkets like Brentwood and Franklin routinely exceeding 90%, drawing consistent lender interest. The development pipeline remains active, particularly in the outer suburbs of Williamson and Rutherford counties, though lenders are closely monitoring construction cost pressures and labor availability for care staff before committing to new ground-up deals.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks with deep Tennessee market knowledge, including Pinnacle Financial Partners and Avenue Bank, are among the most active lenders for stabilized assisted living and memory care acquisitions in Nashville, while debt funds have stepped in aggressively for value-add and transitional assets where conventional lenders pull back. HUD and Fannie Mae agency financing remains a strong option for stabilized, licensed facilities meeting occupancy thresholds, particularly for operators seeking long-term fixed-rate execution in the Franklin and Brentwood corridors.
cities.submarkets: Brentwood, Franklin, Murfreesboro, Germantown, Green Hills, Bellevue, Hendersonville, Nolensville

cities.name: Charlotte
cities.market_notes: Charlotte's senior living and assisted living financing market benefits from one of the fastest-growing 65-plus populations in the Southeast, driven by sustained net in-migration from higher-cost metros and the region's affordability relative to coastal markets. Occupancy rates across assisted living and memory care facilities in the Charlotte metro have rebounded to the mid-to-high 80s, with stabilized Class A properties approaching 90 percent, making the market increasingly attractive to lenders who were cautious during the post-pandemic recovery period. The development pipeline remains active in suburban growth corridors like Ballantyne and Concord, though rising construction costs and longer lease-up timelines have moderated speculative starts and kept underwriting standards disciplined.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks headquartered or with strong Charlotte presences, including Truist Financial and Bank of America, along with debt funds seeking yield in the Southeast, are the most active capital sources for senior living and assisted living facilities in the Charlotte metro right now, drawn by the market's demographic tailwinds and strong operating fundamentals. HUD and Fannie Mae agency financing remain competitive for stabilized, higher-census facilities, while life companies are selectively engaging on well-located, institutional-quality assisted living assets with proven operators.
cities.submarkets: Ballantyne, Concord, University City, Huntersville, Matthews, Pineville, Mooresville, Gastonia

cities.name: Minneapolis
cities.market_notes: Minneapolis-St. Paul is one of the strongest senior living financing markets in the Midwest, supported by a rapidly aging baby boomer population, a high-income retiree base tied to Fortune 500 corporate pensions and healthcare sector employment, and consistently strong occupancy rates that have rebounded well above national averages post-pandemic. The Twin Cities metro benefits from a deeply diversified economy anchored by major healthcare systems including Allina Health and Fairview, which drive ancillary demand for memory care and assisted living facilities in surrounding residential corridors. Development pipeline activity remains measured, with new construction concentrated in affluent suburban nodes, keeping supply-demand dynamics relatively favorable for lenders and operators alike.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including U.S. Bank and Associated Bank are among the most active lenders for senior living and assisted living facilities in the Minneapolis metro, drawn by the market's strong operator track records and stable income fundamentals, while HUD and agency programs through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain highly competitive for stabilized facilities with seasoned occupancy. Debt funds are increasingly stepping in for value-add acquisitions and lease-up bridge scenarios, particularly for memory care projects in suburban submarkets where conventional lenders remain cautious on unstabilized assets.
cities.submarkets: Eden Prairie, Bloomington, Edina, Plymouth, Minnetonka, Woodbury, St. Paul, Maple Grove

cities.name: Portland
cities.market_notes: Portland's senior living and assisted living financing market benefits from strong demographic tailwinds, as Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties are projected to see their 75-plus population grow substantially through 2030, sustaining elevated demand for assisted living and memory care beds. Occupancy rates across stabilized Portland-metro senior living communities have trended back toward the mid-to-high 80s following pandemic-era disruptions, though new development has been tempered by high construction costs, labor shortages, and Oregon's complex regulatory environment for care licensing. Lenders remain selectively interested in well-sponsored, operationally seasoned facilities, but are cautious about lease-up risk on new projects given elevated interest rates and Oregon's history of rent control and tenant-protection legislation extending into the senior housing conversation.

HUD and Fannie Mae agency financing continues to attract attention for stabilized assisted living and memory care facilities seeking long-term, fixed-rate permanent debt, while debt funds have stepped in to fill bridge and value-add lending gaps where conventional banks have tightened underwriting criteria.

Life companies have shown selective interest in institutional-quality communities in Henderson and Summerlin but remain cautious on lease-up assets given the broader national uncertainty around senior housing underwriting.

cities.name: Philadelphia

cities.name: San Antonio
cities.market_notes: San Antonio's senior living market benefits from one of the fastest-growing 65-plus populations in Texas, fueled by military retirees from Fort Sam Houston and Lackland Air Force Base, as well as steady in-migration from higher-cost metros. Occupancy rates across assisted living and memory care facilities have rebounded toward the mid-to-high 80s percent range, drawing renewed lender interest, though the development pipeline in fast-growing corridors like Stone Oak and the Highway 281 corridor has introduced some supply pressure in select submarkets. Lenders remain cautiously optimistic, favoring experienced operators with strong census histories and facilities serving the growing middle-market and value-based care segments that align with San Antonio's affordability profile.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Frost Bank and Cullen/Frost affiliates remain highly active for stabilized assisted living and memory care acquisitions given their familiarity with Texas operators, while debt funds have stepped in to fill construction and bridge financing gaps where conventional lenders have pulled back. HUD and agency financing through FHA 232 programs is gaining traction for larger stabilized facilities seeking long-term fixed-rate execution, particularly for properties with strong Medicaid census given San Antonio's demographics.
cities.submarkets: Stone Oak, Alamo Heights, New Braunfels, Boerne, Northwest San Antonio, Medical Center, Helotes, Northeast San Antonio

cities.name: Raleigh
cities.market_notes: Raleigh-Cary-Durham is one of the strongest senior living markets in the Southeast, driven by sustained in-migration of retirees and pre-retirees attracted to the Research Triangle's quality of life, mild climate, and proximity to world-class healthcare systems including Duke Health and UNC Health. Occupancy rates for stabilized assisted living and memory care facilities in the metro have recovered well above national averages, hovering in the low-to-mid 90s for established operators, making the market highly attractive to both regional and national investors. The development pipeline remains active, particularly in Cary, Morrisville, and the outer Wake County suburbs, though lenders are applying careful underwriting scrutiny to new construction deals given construction cost pressures and lease-up risk in submarkets seeing concentrated supply additions.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks headquartered in the Carolinas, including those with strong North Carolina footprints, are the most consistent lenders for stabilized assisted living and memory care acquisitions, while HUD and Fannie Mae agency financing is actively being deployed for larger, well-occupied facilities seeking long-term fixed-rate debt. Debt funds have stepped in aggressively for bridge-to-agency plays and value-add acquisitions where stabilized cash flow is not yet sufficient for agency qualification, filling a gap that traditional balance sheet lenders have been slower to address in this cycle.
cities.submarkets: Cary, Morrisville, North Raleigh, Durham, Chapel Hill, Wake Forest, Apex, Garner

cities.name: Salt Lake City
cities.market_notes: Salt Lake City's senior living and assisted living financing market is supported by strong underlying demand driven by Utah's rapidly aging Baby Boomer cohort, which is expanding faster than the national average as long-term residents age in place across established suburban communities like Sandy and South Jordan. Occupancy rates across assisted living and memory care facilities in the Salt Lake City metro have trended upward, recovering well past pandemic-era lows and approaching stabilized levels in the low-to-mid 90 percent range in top submarkets. Lenders are cautiously optimistic given Utah's favorable regulatory environment and population growth, though the active development pipeline in communities like Lehi and South Salt Lake is drawing scrutiny around near-term supply risk.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks with strong Utah market presence, including local community lenders and credit unions familiar with the state's operator landscape, are among the most active financing sources for stabilized assisted living and memory care assets in the Salt Lake City metro. HUD and agency lenders remain competitive for larger, stabilized independent living and assisted living facilities, while debt funds are stepping in to fill bridge financing needs for value-add acquisitions and new construction lease-up scenarios, particularly in high-growth corridors along the Wasatch Front.
cities.submarkets: Sandy, South Jordan, Lehi, Provo, Draper, Sugar House, Murray, Ogden

cities.name: Columbus
cities.market_notes: Columbus is one of the strongest senior living markets in the Midwest, supported by a rapidly expanding 75-plus population driven by decades of sustained in-migration and a large base of Ohio State University-affiliated retirees and healthcare workers. Occupancy rates across assisted living and memory care facilities in the metro have rebounded strongly post-pandemic, with stabilized assets routinely achieving 88 to 93 percent occupancy, particularly in affluent suburbs like Dublin, New Albany, and Westerville. The development pipeline remains active but disciplined, with most new supply concentrated in higher-acuity memory care and continuing care retirement community formats rather than standard assisted living, which keeps lender appetite relatively healthy across the capital stack.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Huntington National Bank and Fifth Third Bank are among the most active lenders for stabilized senior living assets in Columbus, offering competitive construction-to-permanent structures given their strong knowledge of Ohio operators and local market conditions. Debt funds and bridge lenders are also filling a meaningful role for value-add and lease-up assisted living deals where agency execution is premature, while HUD 232 financing remains attractive for well-stabilized facilities with strong census history seeking long-term fixed-rate debt.
cities.submarkets: Dublin, Westerville, New Albany, Grove City, Gahanna, Powell, Hilliard, Worthington

cities.name: Kansas City
cities.market_notes: Kansas City's senior living and assisted living financing market benefits from a rapidly aging Baby Boomer population across the metro, with adults 65 and older projected to represent a growing share of the region's affordable cost-of-living demographic. Occupancy rates at stabilized assisted living and memory care facilities in the metro have rebounded to the low-to-mid 80% range post-pandemic, with newer purpose-built communities in suburban corridors like Overland Park and Lee's Summit performing closer to 90%. The development pipeline remains measured, as construction cost pressures have tempered speculative starts, which lenders view favorably as it limits oversupply risk in most established submarkets.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks headquartered in or with strong Kansas City presence, including institutions like UMB Bank and Commerce Bank, remain the most active lenders for stabilized assisted living and memory care acquisitions given their familiarity with local operators and market fundamentals. Debt funds are stepping in aggressively for transitional and value-add senior living deals where traditional bank financing is constrained by lease-up risk, while HUD and Fannie Mae agency programs are gaining traction for larger independent living and assisted living communities that can meet occupancy thresholds.
cities.submarkets: Overland Park, Lee's Summit, Olathe, North Kansas City, Country Club Plaza, Leawood, Liberty, Blue Springs

cities.name: Indianapolis
cities.market_notes: Indianapolis benefits from a rapidly aging population base across Marion and Hamilton counties, with adults 75 and older representing one of the fastest-growing demographic cohorts in the metro, driving consistent occupancy gains at stabilized assisted living and memory care facilities that are now averaging in the low-to-mid 80s percent range. The metro's affordable land costs and business-friendly regulatory environment have attracted national senior living operators and regional developers, though the suburban development pipeline in Carmel and Fishers has introduced some near-term lease-up risk that lenders are monitoring closely. Lenders remain broadly constructive on Indianapolis senior living fundamentals given the strong in-migration trends, below-average construction costs relative to coastal markets, and a diversified local economy anchored by life sciences, logistics, and healthcare that supports stable workforce availability for operators.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Midwest-based community and regional institutions remain the most active capital source for stabilized assisted living and memory care acquisitions in Indianapolis, offering competitive terms for experienced operators with proven track records, while HUD and agency lenders through Fannie Mae and FHA are increasingly attractive for larger independent living communities seeking long-term fixed-rate debt. Debt funds have stepped in to fill the bridge lending gap for value-add and lease-up situations in high-growth suburban submarkets where conventional lenders require higher stabilized occupancy thresholds before committing.
cities.submarkets: Carmel, Fishers, Noblesville, Greenwood, Zionsville, Castleton, Lawrence, Avon

cities.name: San Jose
cities.market_notes: San Jose and the broader Silicon Valley corridor represent one of the most compelling senior living financing markets in the nation, driven by an exceptionally affluent aging population with high median household incomes and significant accumulated wealth from decades of tech sector employment and equity appreciation. Occupancy rates across assisted living and memory care facilities in the metro have rebounded strongly above 90% in stabilized assets, reflecting acute undersupply relative to the 65-plus demographic growing fastest in high-income zip codes across Santa Clara County. Development pipelines remain constrained by some of the highest land costs and construction cost burdens in the country, which creates durable rent growth dynamics for existing facilities but also introduces significant underwriting complexity for ground-up deals seeking financing.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Debt funds and bridge lenders are most active in San Jose right now, targeting value-add assisted living and memory care acquisitions where sponsors need flexible, non-recourse capital to execute operational turnarounds in a market where stabilized cash flows command premium valuations. Regional banks including those with strong Northern California footprints are selectively financing stabilized independent living and assisted living assets, while HUD and agency executions through HUD 232 remain attractive for sponsors with the patience to navigate longer timelines given the strong NOI and low cap rate environment.
cities.submarkets: Sunnyvale, Santa Clara, Cupertino, Mountain View, Milpitas, Downtown San Jose, Willow Glen, Almaden Valley
